claim: Gregarious locusts exhibit intense black patterns with a ventral brown color.
source: The gregarious locusts exhibited intense black patterns with a ventral brown color, and the solitary locusts showed the expected uniform green coloration (Figure 1A).
evidence: Directly stated in the text and shown in Figure 1A which displays the body colors of typical gregarious and solitary nymphs.

claim: Solitary locusts show uniform green coloration.
source: The gregarious locusts exhibited intense black patterns with a ventral brown color, and the solitary locusts showed the expected uniform green coloration (Figure 1A).
evidence: Directly stated in the text and shown in Figure 1A which displays the body colors of typical gregarious and solitary nymphs.

claim: A total of 1653 differentially expressed genes (DEGs) were identified between gregarious and solitary locusts.
source: We identified a total of 1653 DEGs between the gregarious and solitary locusts (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A)
evidence: Stated in the text with reference to transcriptome sequencing data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: 26% (430) of the 1653 DEGs were protein-coding genes.
source: 26% (430) of these DEGs were protein-coding genes (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Stated in the text with reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 1B showing the numbers of annotated genes among DEGs.

claim: Sixty-eight of the 430 protein-coding DEGs are involved in pathways associated with animal coloration.
source: Sixty-eight of the 430 protein-coding DEGs are involved in pathways associated with animal coloration (Figure 1B).
evidence: Stated in the text with reference to Figure 1B showing the volcano plot of DEGs associated with animal coloration.

claim: After molting, the dark pattern in the pronotum decreased markedly in 60% of the gregarious locusts after βCBP knockdown.
source: After molting, the dark pattern in the pronotum decreased markedly in 60% of the gregarious locusts after βCBP knockdown (Figure 1D).
evidence: Stated in the text with reference to Figure 1D showing the effects of βCBP dsRNA treatment on body color.

claim: βCBP was predominantly expressed in the locust integument tissue.
source: we performed quantitative reverse transcriptase–polymerase chain reaction (qRT–PCR) and found that βCBP was predominantly expressed in the locust integument tissue (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Stated in the text with reference to qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: βCBP expression was significantly higher in the pronotum than in the tergum integuments of the thorax and abdomen in gregarious locusts.
source: we found that βCBP expression was significantly higher in the pronotum than in the tergum integuments of the thorax and abdomen in gregarious locusts, whereas little βCBP expression was observed in the terga of solitary locusts, with no variability among the tergum segments (Figure 2A).
evidence: Stated in the text with reference to Figure 2A showing βCBP expression in different body segments.

claim: The βCBP transcript level increased with developmental stage in gregarious locusts.
source: The βCBP transcript level increased with developmental stage, with the expression levels of 4th instar gregarious locusts being approximately 200 times those of the 2nd and 3rd instar gregarious locusts.
evidence: Stated in the text describing qRT-PCR results across developmental stages.

claim: βCBP expression was invariable across the developmental stages in solitary locusts.
source: By contrast, βCBP expression was invariable across the developmental stages in solitary locusts (Figure 2B).
evidence: Stated in the text with reference to Figure 2B showing βCBP expression across developmental stages.

claim: The extent of black body coloration in locusts is positively correlated with βCBP expression level.
source: Therefore, the extent of black body coloration in locusts is positively correlated with βCBP expression level.
evidence: Stated as a conclusion based on the qRT-PCR data showing βCBP expression patterns correlating with body color.

claim: The transcript level of βCBP was significantly higher in the pronotum and tergum integuments of the thorax and abdomen of gregarious individuals than the pronotum and tergum integuments of solitary individuals.
source: The transcript level of βCBP was significantly higher in the pronotum and tergum integuments of the thorax and abdomen of gregarious individuals than the pronotum and tergum integuments of solitary individuals (Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Stated in the text with reference to qPCR data shown in Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: Isolating the gregarious locusts (IG) significantly decreased the transcript level of βCBP.
source: Moreover, isolating the gregarious locusts (IG) significantly decreased the transcript level of βCBP (Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplements 2 and 3).
evidence: Stated in the text with reference to qPCR data shown in Figure 2C and supplementary figures.

claim: Crowding the solitary locusts (CS) significantly increased the transcript level of βCBP.
source: By contrast, crowding the solitary locusts (CS) significantly increased the transcript level of βCBP (Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Stated in the text with reference to qPCR data shown in Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: The level of CBP protein in the locust pronotum integuments was significantly higher in the gregarious locusts than in the solitary locusts.
source: We also found that the level of CBP protein in the locust pronotum integuments was significantly higher in the gregarious locusts than in the solitary locusts (Figure 2D).
evidence: Stated in the text with reference to Western blot data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The protein levels of βCBP declined when the locusts were isolated and increased under the crowding conditions.
source: Moreover, the protein levels of βCBP declined when the locusts were isolated and increased under the crowding conditions (Figure 2D).
evidence: Stated in the text with reference to Western blot data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Large amounts of βCBP were widely detected in the intercellular space of the pronotum of gregarious locusts.
source: We found that large amounts of βCBP were widely detected in the intercellular space of the pronotum of gregarious locusts, whereas βCBP was distributed very sporadically in the solitary locusts (Figure 2E).
evidence: Stated in the text with reference to immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: βCBP was distributed very sporadically in the solitary locusts.
source: We found that large amounts of βCBP were widely detected in the intercellular space of the pronotum of gregarious locusts, whereas βCBP was distributed very sporadically in the solitary locusts (Figure 2E).
evidence: Stated in the text with reference to immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: The amount of βCBP protein in the pronotum of gregarious locusts was 39.5-fold higher than the corresponding amount in solitary locusts.
source: The amount of βCBP protein in the pronotum of gregarious locusts was 39.5-fold higher than the corresponding amount in solitary locusts (Figure 2G).
evidence: Stated in the text with reference to quantified fluorescence intensity data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: The β-carotene content in the gregarious locusts was 2.8-fold higher than that in the solitary locusts.
source: The β-carotene content in the gregarious locusts was 2.8-fold higher than that in the solitary locusts (Figure 2H).
evidence: Stated in the text with reference to HPLC data shown in Figure 2H.

claim: βCBP protein level and the associated β-carotene content are directly correlated with the degree of black coloration of the locust pronotum.
source: These results suggest that βCBP protein level and the associated β-carotene content are directly correlated with the degree of black coloration of the locust pronotum.
evidence: Stated as a conclusion based on the combined data from protein and β-carotene measurements.

claim: After injection of dsβCBP–RNA and isolation treatment, the mRNA and protein levels of βCBP in the pronotum integument decreased by 99% and 85%, respectively, relative to the levels in dsGFP–RNA-injected and isolated controls.
source: After injection of dsβCBP–RNA and isolation treatment, the mRNA and protein levels of βCBP in the pronotum integument decreased by 99% and 85%, respectively, relative to the levels in dsGFP–RNA-injected and isolated controls (Figure 3A and C).
evidence: Stated in the text with reference to qPCR and Western blot data shown in Figure 3A and C.

claim: The mRNA levels of βCBP in the tergum of the thorax and abdomen decreased by 98% relative to the levels in dsGFP–RNA-injected and isolated controls.
source: In addition, the mRNA levels of βCBP in the tergum of the thorax and abdomen decreased by 98% relative to the levels in dsGFP–RNA-injected and isolated controls (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Stated in the text with reference to qPCR data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The silencing effect of dsβCBP–RNA resulted in an 80% decrease in the signal intensity of βCBP in the pronotum integuments of gregarious locusts relative to the corresponding intensity in the dsGFP–RNA injected controls.
source: The silencing effect of dsβCBP–RNA resulted in an 80% decrease in the signal intensity of βCBP in the pronotum integuments of gregarious locusts relative to the corresponding intensity in the dsGFP–RNA injected controls (Figure 3E and F).
evidence: Stated in the text with reference to immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 3E and F.

claim: The administration of dsβCBP significantly reduced the β-carotene content in the pronotum integuments from 104.8 μg/g to 74.3 μg/g.
source: The administration of dsβCBP significantly reduced the β-carotene content in the pronotum integuments from 104.8 μg/g to 74.3 μg/g (*p < 0.05, Figure 3H).
evidence: Stated in the text with reference to HPLC data shown in Figure 3H.

claim: 48% of the nymphs injected with dsβCBP–RNA and then isolated showed substantial lightening of the black pronotum.
source: A body coloration assay revealed that after molting of 29 locusts, 48% of the nymphs injected with dsβCBP–RNA and then isolated showed substantial lightening of the black pronotum.
evidence: Stated in the text describing the results of the body coloration assay.

claim: 41% of the gregarious nymphs shifted to a complete green-colored body after dsβCBP–RNA injection and isolation.
source: Moreover, 41% of the gregarious nymphs shifted to a complete green-colored body.
evidence: Stated in the text describing the results of the body coloration assay.

claim: 73% of the dsGFP–RNA-injected gregarious nymphs treated with isolation retained an intense black body pattern.
source: By contrast, 73% of the dsGFP–RNA-injected gregarious nymphs treated with isolation retained an intense black body pattern.
evidence: Stated in the text describing the control group results.

claim: Only 27% of the dsGFP-injected and isolated control locusts showed body color lightening.
source: Only 27% of the dsGFP-injected and isolated control locusts showed body color lightening (Figure 4A).
evidence: Stated in the text with reference to Figure 4A showing the effects of βCBP dsRNA treatment.

claim: βCBP regulates the body color changes of gregarious and solitary locusts between black and green coloration.
source: These results support the view that βCBP regulates the body color changes of gregarious and solitary locusts between black and green coloration.
evidence: Stated as a conclusion based on the RNAi knockdown experiments.

claim: The mRNA and protein levels of βCBP significantly increased by 11.2- and 2.5-fold in the pronotum, respectively, after β-carotene feeding and crowding.
source: The mRNA and protein levels of βCBP significantly increased by 11.2- and 2.5-fold in the pronotum, respectively, and increased by 2.3- and 2.1-fold in the tergum of the thorax and abdomen, respectively, relative to the corresponding levels in the regular diet-fed and crowded controls (Figure 3B,D and Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Stated in the text with reference to qPCR and Western blot data shown in Figure 3B, D and Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: The signal intensity of βCBP increased by 22.7-fold in the pronotum integument cells of the solitary locusts after β-carotene feeding and crowding.
source: Moreover, the signal intensity of βCBP increased by 22.7-fold in the pronotum integument cells of the solitary locusts after β-carotene feeding and crowding relative to the intensity in the regular diet-fed and crowded controls (Figure 3E and G).
evidence: Stated in the text with reference to immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 3E and G.

claim: The amount of βCBP–β-carotene complex in the solitary integuments increased by 3.4-fold after β-carotene feeding and crowding.
source: In addition, HPLC analysis revealed that the amount of βCBP–β-carotene complex in the solitary integuments increased by 3.4-fold after β-carotene feeding and crowding (Figure 3H).
evidence: Stated in the text with reference to HPLC data shown in Figure 3H.

claim: 47% of the solitary locusts completely shifted to the typical gregarious body color after feeding with β-carotene and crowding.
source: A total of 47% of the solitary locusts completely shifted to the typical gregarious body color, and the pronota of 33% of the feeding locusts developed extensive black areas similar to the gregarious body color after feeding with β-carotene and crowding.
evidence: Stated in the text describing the results of the β-carotene feeding experiment.

claim: 33% of the feeding locusts developed extensive black areas similar to the gregarious body color after feeding with β-carotene and crowding.
source: A total of 47% of the solitary locusts completely shifted to the typical gregarious body color, and the pronota of 33% of the feeding locusts developed extensive black areas similar to the gregarious body color after feeding with β-carotene and crowding.
evidence: Stated in the text describing the results of the β-carotene feeding experiment.

claim: 87% of the locusts retained their green color in the regular diet and crowding treatment (control group).
source: However, 87% of the locusts retained their green color in the regular diet and crowding treatment (control group) (Figure 4B).
evidence: Stated in the text with reference to Figure 4B showing the effects of β-carotene feeding.

claim: βCBP and β-carotene can jointly induce body color changes from green to black associated with phase transition in the locusts.
source: Thus, βCBP and β-carotene can jointly induce body color changes from green to black associated with phase transition in the locusts.
evidence: Stated as a conclusion based on the β-carotene feeding experiments.

claim: 35.5% of the dsβCBP-injected nymphs pre-fed with β-carotene showed green body color.
source: After molting, 35.5% of the dsβCBP-injected nymphs pre-fed with β-carotene showed green body color, whereas 15.6% of the green individuals in the dsGFP-injected group pre-fed with β-carotene did so.
evidence: Stated in the text describing the results of the rescue experiment.

claim: 15.6% of the green individuals in the dsGFP-injected group pre-fed with β-carotene showed green body color.
source: After molting, 35.5% of the dsβCBP-injected nymphs pre-fed with β-carotene showed green body color, whereas 15.6% of the green individuals in the dsGFP-injected group pre-fed with β-carotene did so.
evidence: Stated in the text describing the results of the rescue experiment.

claim: The phenotype of black tergum individuals induced by β-carotene was rescued only by injection with dsβCBP-RNA.
source: Correspondingly, the phenotype of black tergum individuals induced by β-carotene was rescued only by injection with dsβCBP-RNA (Figure 4C).
evidence: Stated in the text with reference to Figure 4C showing the rescue experiment results.

claim: βCBP acts with β-carotene to regulate the black body color of gregarious locusts.
source: Therefore, βCBP acts with β-carotene to regulate the black body color of gregarious locusts, and β-carotene by oneself did not regulate the body color.
evidence: Stated as a conclusion based on the rescue experiment results.

claim: β-carotene by itself did not regulate the body color.
source: Therefore, βCBP acts with β-carotene to regulate the black body color of gregarious locusts, and β-carotene by oneself did not regulate the body color.
evidence: Stated as a conclusion based on the rescue experiment results.

claim: Immunoprecipitation of β-carotene-rβCBP formed a red complex.
source: Immunoprecipitation of β-carotene-rβCBP formed a red complex, whereas no red precipitate formed when β-carotene was added to bovine serum albumin (BSA) or when β-carotene in the absence of rβCBP was incubated in the binding buffer followed by immunoprecipitation (Figure 5A).
evidence: Stated in the text with reference to Figure 5A showing the pigment immunoprecipitation assay in vitro.

claim: No red precipitate formed when β-carotene was added to bovine serum albumin (BSA).
source: Immunoprecipitation of β-carotene-rβCBP formed a red complex, whereas no red precipitate formed when β-carotene was added to bovine serum albumin (BSA) or when β-carotene in the absence of rβCBP was incubated in the binding buffer followed by immunoprecipitation (Figure 5A).
evidence: Stated in the text with reference to Figure 5A showing the pigment immunoprecipitation assay in vitro.

claim: No red precipitate formed when β-carotene in the absence of rβCBP was incubated in the binding buffer followed by immunoprecipitation.
source: Immunoprecipitation of β-carotene-rβCBP formed a red complex, whereas no red precipitate formed when β-carotene was added to bovine serum albumin (BSA) or when β-carotene in the absence of rβCBP was incubated in the binding buffer followed by immunoprecipitation (Figure 5A).
evidence: Stated in the text with reference to Figure 5A showing the pigment immunoprecipitation assay in vitro.

claim: The pigment immunoprecipitation assay in vivo showed an accumulation of red pigment in the precipitate of the integument when treated with anti-βCBP-immunoprecipitation compared with IgG-immunoprecipitation.
source: The pigment immunoprecipitation assay in vivo also showed an accumulation of red pigment in the precipitate of the integument when treated with anti-βCBP-immunoprecipitation compared with IgG-immunoprecipitation (Figure 5B).
evidence: Stated in the text with reference to Figure 5B showing the pigment immunoprecipitation assay in vivo.

claim: The red pigment in the βCBP precipitant results from β-carotene.
source: Furthermore, we confirmed that the red pigment in the βCBP precipitant result from β-carotene by HPLC analysis (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Stated in the text with reference to HPLC data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: βCBP directly binds with β-carotene in the pronotum integument to form the red complex, which directly contributes to the black pattern of the pronotum in gregarious locusts.
source: These results provide strong evidence that βCBP directly binds with β-carotene in the pronotum integument to form the red complex, which directly contributes to the black pattern of the pronotum in gregarious locusts.
evidence: Stated as a conclusion based on the immunoprecipitation assays.

claim: The gold particles were present mainly in the pigment granules of the pronotum integuments.
source: The gold particles were present mainly in the pigment granules of the pronotum integuments.
evidence: Stated in the text describing the immunoelectron microscopy results.

claim: The average number of gold particles in the pigment granules from the pronotum integuments was 15.5-fold higher in the gregarious locusts than in the solitary locusts.
source: In addition, the average number of gold particles in the pigment granules from the pronotum integuments was 15.5-fold higher in the gregarious locusts than in the solitary locusts (Figure 5C and F).
evidence: Stated in the text with reference to immunoelectron microscopy data shown in Figure 5C and F.

claim: βCBP silencing coupled with isolation caused a severe deficiency of gold particles in the pigment granules of the gregarious locusts.
source: Furthermore, βCBP silencing coupled with isolation caused a severe deficiency of gold particles in the pigment granules of the gregarious locusts, indicating a substantial reduction in the βCBP protein–pigment complex relative to the level in the dsGFP-injected and isolated controls (Figure 5D and G).
evidence: Stated in the text with reference to immunoelectron microscopy data shown in Figure 5D and G.

claim: β-carotene intake coupled with crowding evidently increased the gold particles responsible for the βCBP production in the pigment granules of pronotum in the solitary locusts.
source: By contrast, β-carotene intake coupled with crowding evidently increased the gold particles responsible for the βCBP production in the pigment granules of pronotum in the solitary locusts, demonstrating a significant promotion of βCBP protein–pigment complex accumulation compared with accumulation in the regular diet-fed and crowded controls (Figure 5E and H).
evidence: Stated in the text with reference to immunoelectron microscopy data shown in Figure 5E and H.

claim: The βCBP–pigment complex is a key mediator of black formation in the pronotum integuments of gregarious locusts.
source: Thus, the βCBP–pigment complex is a key mediator of black formation in the pronotum integuments of gregarious locusts.
evidence: Stated as a conclusion based on the immunoelectron microscopy results.

source: The black–brown pattern in the gregarious locusts resulted from the superposition or balancing effect of a red pigment on the green background of solitary locusts rather than complete melanogenesis.

claim: Crowding treatment increased the βCBP levels in the integuments and caused body color change in the solitary locusts by the binding of βCBP with β-carotenes.
source: Crowding treatment increased the βCBP levels in the integuments and caused body color change in the solitary locusts by the binding of βCBP with β-carotenes (Figure 6).

claim: This finding of animal coloration corresponds precisely with the physically trichromatic rule.
source: This finding of animal coloration corresponds precisely with the physically trichromatic rule.
evidence: Stated in the Discussion section as an interpretation of the findings.

claim: βCBP expression is not only positively correlated with the black color of the pronotum in gregarious locusts but also phase-related in response to population density changes.
source: We demonstrated that βCBP expression is not only positively correlated with the black color of the pronotum in gregarious locusts but also phase-related in response to population density changes.

claim: The βCBP expression in solitary locusts was not induced by merely feeding with β-carotene without crowding treatment.
source: The βCBP expression in solitary locusts was not induced by merely feeding with β-carotene without crowding treatment (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Stated in the Discussion section with reference to Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: Population density of locusts acts as necessary and sufficient condition to drive the changes of body coloration.
source: Thus, population density of locusts acts as necessary and sufficient condition to drive the changes of body coloration.
evidence: Stated in the Discussion section as a conclusion based on the experimental results.

claim: The melanocortin-1 receptor gene regulates melanin production associated with black hair and skin in human and mouse pigmentation responsed to ultraviolet-light.
source: For instance, the melanocortin-1 receptor gene regulates melanin production associated with black hair and skin in human and mouse pigmentation responsed to ultraviolet-light (D'Orazio et al., 2006).
evidence: Stated in the Discussion section with a citation to D'Orazio et al., 2006.

claim: The major honest signaling of red carotenoids in Zebrafinch is thought to be the beak, colored in orange thanks to the ketolase activity encoded by the cytochrome P450 gene which was recruited from an ancestral function in retinal oil droplets.
source: The major honest signaling of red carotenoids in Zebrafinch (Mundy et al., 2016) is thought to be the beak, colored in orange thanks to the ketolase activity encoded by the cytochrome P450 gene which was recruited from an ancestral function in retinal oil droplets.

source: In our study, single βCBP or β-carotene cannot produce pigment deposition in the black tergum integuments of the locusts.

source: βCBP only combine β-carotene to form red pigment complex for producing the black pattern of gregarious locusts.

source: In the silkworm Bombyx mori, the yellow cocoon color is determined by the carotenoid-binding protein gene, which controls the uptake of carotenoids in the silk gland (Sakudoh et al., 2007).

claim: Carotenoid-binding protein mutation produces colorless hemolymph and white cocoons.
source: Carotenoid-binding protein mutation produces colorless hemolymph and white cocoons, indicating that carotenoid-binding protein plays a central role in cocoon color pigmentation (Sakudoh et al., 2007; Wang et al., 2014a).

claim: Mammals often obtain carotenoids by eating plants.
source: Mammals often obtain carotenoids by eating plants (Avalos and Carmen Limón, 2015; Bryon et al., 2017; Toews et al., 2017).
evidence: Stated in the Discussion section with citations to Avalos and Carmen Limón, 2015; Bryon et al., 2017; Toews et al., 2017.

source: Once absorbed, carotenoids are transported by lipoproteins, which are homologs of CBP in insects, through the bloodstream to the target tissues.

source: Interestingly, β-carotene-binding protein, as a key mediator of body color production, controls β-carotene content and absorption to produce red color, which is superposed on the background color of gregarious locus to yield the black pattern.

source: Our results show that the black pattern of gregarious locusts is caused by the interaction and mixture of different pigments.

source: This pigment interaction has a colored palette effect that results in black coloration due to the accumulation of red color β-carotene pigments in the presence of blue and yellow pigments.

source: The disappearance of the red pigment in the gregarious locusts led to the emergence of green color, which is the typical body color of solitary locusts.

source: Parrots acquire their colors through regulatory changes that drive the high expression of MuPKS in feather epithelia, which appear green when the blue and yellow pigments are present (Cooke et al., 2017).

claim: The green color of the integument in two species of locusts, the migratory locust and desert locust (Schistocerca gregaria) is obtained from a mixture of blue biliverdin pigment and yellow carotenoids.
source: The green color of the integument in two species of locusts, the migratory locust and desert locust (Schistocerca gregaria) is obtained from a mixture of blue biliverdin pigment and yellow carotenoids (Goodwin, 1952; Goodwin and Srisukh, 1951).

claim: Carotenoid binding protein plays a key role in the yellow cocoon pigmentation by binding with yellow carotenoids.
source: For example, carotenoid binding protein plays a key role in the yellow cocoon pigmentation by binding with yellow carotenoids (Tabunoki et al., 2004).

claim: The expression levels of a biliverdin-binding protein and a carotenoid-binding protein in the pronotum integument were not significantly different between the gregarious and solitary locusts.

claim: The contents of blue biliverdin and yellow carotenoid are the same in gregarious and solitary locusts.

claim: The change from typical gregarious-phased coloration (black) to solitary-phased coloration (green) is dependent on the extent of red β-carotene bound to βCBP.
source: Thus, our results suggest a colored palette mechanism of body color change, with the change from typical gregarious-phased coloration (black) to solitary-phased coloration (green) is dependent on the extent of red β-carotene bound to βCBP.
